source.title: Scaling and Renormalization in Neural Networks: An Effective Renormalization-Group Description of Grokking
source.authors: Min Chen; Jun-Qin Wang; Ze-Guan Wu; Wen-Hao Huang; Jun-Yu Liu

record.tranche_reason: The study measures delayed generalization on modular addition, using its own ensemble and scaling analyses rather than presenting an explicit reproduction of the original experiment.
record.gate_note: The study reports results bearing on V1 for modular addition. Its RG, norm, fluctuation, and coupling results do not measure the circuit formation and removal named in V2 or the efficiency account named in V5. Weight decay is varied for the local RG fit, not to test V5. Results cited from other papers are excluded.
record.test_reason: The study trains its own ensemble on modular addition (p = 97, 50% split) and reports test accuracy reaching 99% between epochs 170–182. That bears on V1's delayed, abrupt generalization. The setup differs from Power et al.: a quadratic two-layer MLP with MSE and very large weight decay (λ = 15). The RG, norm, fluctuation and exponent results do not address the circuit (V2), the data-type or initialization switch (V3), LLMs (V4), the efficiency account or ungrokking (V5), algorithm identity (V6) or artifacts (V7).
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly correct. The authors conclude that a scaling/RG framework gives a consistent effective, quantitative description of grokking. RG-predicted exponents match direct estimates within 1–10%. ν from the seven-modulus scan matches within 3%, the transition curves collapse under the RG exponent, and the Josephson relation gives an effective dimension near 1. They frame the thermodynamic quantities as effective proxies, not equilibrium quantities.
record.recipe_differences: The study describes modular addition with a 50% random split as following the standard setup, but uses a bias-free two-layer quadratic network with N = 500, full-batch MSE, and AdamW; it does not describe itself as an explicit replication.
record.method_sensitivity: The modulus scan reports transition curves and widths across seven task moduli. The local RG fit also varies epoch and weight decay, but those variations are used to fit the coupling map rather than to test whether weight decay changes grokking delays.

fits_no_version.finding: Cross-run variance of the total squared weight norm (χS) peaks at epoch 118, before the test-accuracy transition at ec = 145.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Ensemble fluctuations of weight norm peak before the generalization jump and could serve as an early indicator of grokking.

fits_no_version.finding: Critical exponents estimated directly (α, β, γ, ν, δ) agree with those from a local RG map within 1.2–9.7%. Transition width across seven moduli scales with ν ≈ 1.40.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The grokking transition shows finite-size scaling, with exponents consistent with an effective one-dimensional RG description.

record.problems: The principal ensemble has 30 runs, and each seed varies both initialization and dataset split, so their contributions are not separated. The authors characterize cross-run thermodynamic quantities as effective proxies, not equilibrium quantities. Only one training fraction is used for the main experiment; the modulus scan does not directly test delay versus training-set size.
record.rows_left_out: No additional eligible results on the claim were identified. The paper's other reported observables concern norms, loss fluctuations, neuron couplings, or RG exponents rather than the claimed circuit mechanism or efficiency account.

untested.parts: Whether the delay grows as the training set shrinks: only a 50% split is used. The modulus scan changes p, and with it the number of training pairs, but it confounds data size with task size. The epoch at which training accuracy saturates is not stated numerically.

missing.what: Mean pseudo-transition epoch ⟨e50⟩p as a function of modulus p, fitted as e∞ + a p^−κ with κ = 2.21. With a fixed 50% split, larger p means more training pairs, so this bears indirectly on delay versus data size. The direction cannot be read from the text and is confounded with task size.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. Grokking serves mainly as a testbed for the RG framework, and the V1 evidence is a by-product of the training setup. The very large weight decay (λ = 15) and short total training (about 250 epochs) mean the delay may be modest; the training-accuracy saturation epoch is figure-only. Weight decay is varied only over λ = 13–17, to fit the RG map and δ, and no delay or ungrokking measure is reported against it, so V5 is untested. Seeds vary initialization and data split together.

versions.untested_parts: The study uses one 50% training split and does not directly test whether the optimization delay grows as the training set shrinks. Its modulus scan measures transition width and curve collapse, not that delay.

rows.value: All 30 runs achieve 99% test accuracy between epochs 170 and 182.
rows.note: The text also describes test performance as suppressed before rising abruptly; it does not give a numerical chance baseline.
rows.check: The 'suppressed before rising abruptly' description in the note is the Introduction's general definition. The study's own number is all 30 runs reaching 99% test accuracy in epochs 170–182. No chance baseline is given.

source_check.locator_found: Section 3.1, task/model/ensemble paragraph; transition-landmarks paragraph; Figure 2A.

rows.subject: two-layer perceptron
rows.operation_detail: Locate the maximum slope of the ensemble-mean test-accuracy curve.
rows.measure: Epoch of maximum slope in mean test accuracy
rows.note: The study identifies this as a transition landmark; the 99% test-accuracy epochs are reported separately in r2.
rows.check: ec = 145 is a landmark the analysis aligns to (maximum slope of mean test accuracy). On its own it does not show a delay relative to training-accuracy saturation.

rows.subject: two-layer perceptron
rows.operation_detail: Scan task modulus and compare transition curves and pseudo-transition widths.
rows.measure: Finite-size scaling of test-accuracy transition width
rows.value: Direct ν = 1.400 from seven moduli; text states the relative spread of e50 scales as p^−1/ν.
rows.note: This reports transition-width scaling, not whether the delay after training accuracy saturation increases as the training set shrinks.
rows.check: Direct ν = 1.400 is a fitted critical exponent from the spread of transition widths across moduli. It is not a measure of delay or of generalization relative to training set size.

rows.subject: two-layer perceptron
rows.operation_detail: Rescale test-accuracy curves and compare the transition-collapse fits across candidate exponents.
rows.value: Rescaling with νRG = 1.444 produces data collapse; collapse cost is minimized at ν = 1.50 for mean accuracy curves.
rows.note: The text reports collapse across moduli; this result does not establish how the overfitting-to-generalization delay changes with training-set size.
rows.check: Curve collapse and the collapse-cost minimum are fit-quality results for the study's own RG exponent. They are not a measure of the grokking delay.
